pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.3.2)
- B9.3.2.2 — Solve problems involving bearings and the addition and subtraction of vectors.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- state and use the conditions for two vectors to be parallel or perpendicular
- apply the triangle law of vector addition
- apply the parallelogram law of vector addition
- use vectors to solve problems on triangles and parallelograms

lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular vectors

pages.title: Parallel and perpendicular vectors
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Show an understanding of parallel vectors and perpendicular vectors.
Curriculum indicator B9.3.2.2.1
> 🧪 **Activity 11.1 — Investigating vectors**
On squared paper draw **a** = col{2;1}, **b** = col{4;2}, **c** = col{−6;−3} and **d** = col{−1;2}.
1. Which vectors point along the same line (parallel)? How are their components related?
2. Measure the angle between **a** and **d**. Work out (2 × −1) + (1 × 2). What do you notice?
> 🔑 **Key idea: Parallel vectors** — Two vectors are **parallel** if one is a **scalar multiple** of the other: **b** = k**a**. In components, col{a;b} ∥ col{c;d} when [[a/c]] = [[b/d]] (equivalently **ad = bc**). If k is negative the vectors point in opposite directions.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Perpendicular vectors** — Two vectors col{a;b} and col{c;d} are **perpendicular** (at 90°) when **ac + bd = 0**. For example col{2;1} ⊥ col{−1;2} because 2(−1) + 1(2) = 0. A quick way to make a perpendicular vector: swap the components and change one sign: col{a;b} ⊥ col{−b;a}.
[[fig:m9-f29|Figure 11.1: Parallel and perpendicular vectors]]
## ✏️ Example 11.1
a) Find the value(s) of x if the vectors col{x;3} and col{12;x} are parallel. b) Which of the vectors is perpendicular to col{3;4}? (a) col{−3;4} (b) col{−3;−4} (c) col{−4;3} (d) col{−4;−3}
**Solution**
a) Parallel ⟹ x × x = 3 × 12 ⟹ x² = 36 ⟹ **x = 6 or x = −6**. (For x = 6: col{12;6} = 2col{6;3} ✓.)
b) Test ac + bd with col{3;4}:
(a) 3(−3) + 4(4) = 7 (b) 3(−3) + 4(−4) = −25 (c) 3(−4) + 4(3) = **0** (d) 3(−4) + 4(−3) = −24
Only **(c)** col{−4;3} is perpendicular to col{3;4}.

pages.title: Exercise 11.1
pages.body:

1. Which pairs are parallel? a) col{2;5} and col{6;15} b) col{1;−3} and col{−2;6} c) col{4;2} and col{2;4}
2. Find k if col{k;6} is parallel to col{2;3}.
3. Find m if col{m;2} is perpendicular to col{3;−6}.
4. Show that the points A(1, 2), B(3, 6) and C(6, 12) lie on a straight line (Hint: show vec{AB} ∥ vec{BC}).

questions.q: Find k if col{k;6} is parallel to col{2;3}.
Find m if col{m;2} is perpendicular to col{3;−6}.
Show that the points A(1, 2), B(3, 6) and C(6, 12) lie on a straight line (Hint: show vec{AB} ∥ vec{BC}).

parts.a: vec{AB} = col{2;4}, vec{BC} = col{3;6} = 1.5vec{AB}: parallel with B in common, so A, B, C are collinear.

pages.title: The triangle and parallelogram laws
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply the triangle and parallelogram laws of addition to resolve vectors.
Curriculum indicator B9.3.2.2.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Triangle law** — If two vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle taken **in order** (nose to tail), their sum is represented by the third side taken the other way: vec{AB} **+** vec{BC} **=** vec{AC}.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Parallelogram law** — If two vectors **a** and **b** start from the **same point** and form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their sum **a** + **b** is the **diagonal** of the parallelogram from that point.
[[fig:m9-f30|Figure 11.2: The triangle law and the parallelogram law]]
## ✏️ Example 11.2
The vertices of a triangle are P(1, −3), Q(7, 5) and R(−3, 5). a) Express vec{PQ}, vec{QR} and vec{PR} as column vectors and verify the triangle law. b) Show that triangle PQR is isosceles. c) Find the equation of the line PR.
**Solution**
a) vec{PQ} = col{7 − 1;5 − (−3)} = col{6;8}; vec{QR} = col{−3 − 7;5 − 5} = col{−10;0}; vec{PR} = col{−4;8}.
Check: vec{PQ} + vec{QR} = col{6 − 10;8 + 0} = col{−4;8} = vec{PR} ✓
b) |vec{PQ}| = √(36 + 64) = 10; |vec{QR}| = 10; |vec{PR}| = √(16 + 64) = √80 ≈ 8.94. Two sides are equal, so **△PQR is isosceles** (PQ = QR = 10).
c) Gradient of PR = [[8/−4]] = −2. Through P(1, −3): y + 3 = −2(x − 1) ⟹ **y = −2x − 1**. (Check R: −2(−3) − 1 = 5 ✓)

pages.title: Example 11.3
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 11.3
PQRS is a parallelogram with vertices P(x, y), Q(5, 7), R(2, 4) and S(1, 3). Find vec{PQ} and vec{SR}, and hence x and y.
**Solution**
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel, so vec{PQ} = vec{SR}.
vec{SR} = col{2 − 1;4 − 3} = col{1;1}; vec{PQ} = col{5 − x;7 − y}
5 − x = 1 ⟹ **x = 4**; 7 − y = 1 ⟹ **y = 6**
So P is (4, 6). Check with the parallelogram law: vec{PS} + vec{PQ} = col{−3;−3} + col{1;1} = col{−2;−2} = vec{PR} ✓
> 🌍 **Maths in real life** Vectors are used to combine forces and velocities. A boat heading across a river at 4 m/s while the current flows at 3 m/s actually moves at sqrt{4^{2} + 3^{2}} = 5 m/s — the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two velocities.

pages.title: Exercise 11.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 11.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A(2, 1), B(5, 5) and C(9, 2). Find vec{AB}, vec{BC} and vec{AC} and verify that vec{AB} + vec{BC} = vec{AC}. Is the triangle isosceles?
2. ABCD is a parallelogram with A(1, 1), B(4, 2) and D(2, 4). Find C.
3. Two forces col{5;2} N and col{1;6} N act at a point. Find the resultant force and its magnitude.
4. Show that A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(5, 5) and D(1, 4) form a parallelogram. Is it a rhombus?

questions.q: A(2, 1), B(5, 5) and C(9, 2). Find vec{AB}, vec{BC} and vec{AC} and verify that vec{AB} + vec{BC} = vec{AC}. Is the triangle isosceles?

parts.a: col{3;4}, col{4;−3}, col{7;1}; |AB| = |BC| = 5, so yes, isosceles (and right-angled at B since 3 × 4 + 4 × (−3) = 0)

questions.q: ABCD is a parallelogram with A(1, 1), B(4, 2) and D(2, 4). Find C.
Two forces col{5;2} N and col{1;6} N act at a point. Find the resultant force and its magnitude.
Show that A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(5, 5) and D(1, 4) form a parallelogram. Is it a rhombus?

parts.a: vec{AB} = vec{DC} = col{4;1} and vec{AD} = vec{BC} = col{1;4}, so it is a parallelogram; all sides √17, so it is a rhombus.

lessons.title: Chapter summary

pages.title: Chapter 11 summary
pages.body:
- Parallel: **b** = k**a** (ad = bc). Perpendicular: ac + bd = 0.
- Triangle law: vec{AB} + vec{BC} = vec{AC}. Parallelogram law: the sum of two vectors from one point is the diagonal.
